title: Harbor Gateway Scheduling Center
event: A cyberattack disables the appointment and gate-scheduling system at a regional container port.
why: The scheduling system tells trucks when to arrive and which containers to move. Without it, the port cannot coordinate arrivals, and cargo begins to back up at the terminal.
how: Trucks arrive without valid appointments, gates slow to manual processing, containers sit longer in the yard, and the terminal fills toward capacity as ships continue to arrive.
when: The risk grows when scheduling software is unpatched, when a single system has no manual backup, or when the port is already near peak volume and has little slack to absorb delay.
where: The first effects appear at the port gates and container yard, then spread to trucking companies, rail connections, warehouses, and the retailers and manufacturers waiting on the cargo.

keyTerms.definition: A scheduled time slot that tells a truck when to arrive at the port to pick up or drop off a container.
keyTerms.example: A carrier books a 9:00 AM slot so its truck is not left waiting at a full gate.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Appointments keep truck arrivals matched to the port's capacity so the gates and yard do not overload.

keyTerms.definition: The number of containers a terminal can hold before it runs out of usable space.
keyTerms.example: A yard near its limit cannot accept new containers until others are moved out.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: When a yard fills up, ships cannot unload and the whole terminal slows down.

keyTerms.definition: A backup process that lets work continue by hand when the normal system is unavailable.
keyTerms.example: Gate staff check paperwork manually when the digital scheduling system is offline.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A manual fallback keeps essential movement going, but usually at a much slower rate than the automated system.

question: Which response best keeps priority cargo moving while the scheduling system is offline?
options: Keep accepting all trucks at normal volume and sort it out at the gate
Switch to manual gate processing, meter truck arrivals, and prioritize essential and time-sensitive containers
Close the gates completely until the scheduling system is restored
optionRationales: Normal volume without scheduling overwhelms manual gates and fills the yard, making the backlog worse.
This response keeps the port moving at a safe rate and protects the most important cargo while the system is repaired.
A full closure stops the backlog from growing but also halts essential and perishable cargo that could still move slowly.
takeaway: When a scheduling system fails, meter arrivals to the manual processing rate and move the most important cargo first.
responsePrinciple: Fall back to manual processing, match truck arrivals to real capacity, and protect priority cargo.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The ship cannot discharge because the container yard is backing up.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Manual processing is metering arrivals, so priority containers clear and the vessel is re-sequenced to discharge.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The gates are closed, so the vessel waits with no discharge slot.

cascadeSteps: A cyberattack disables the port scheduling system.
Trucks arrive without appointments and gates fall back to slow manual processing.
Containers accumulate in the yard as it approaches capacity.
Warehouses, rail connections, and waiting retailers receive their cargo late.

intelligence.confirmed: Port scheduling and gate systems are unavailable, and staff have activated manual processing.
intelligence.uncertainty: The restoration time, attack scope, system integrity, yard capacity, and size of the developing backlog remain uncertain.
intelligence.verificationFinding: Determine whether the attack is contained to the scheduling environment and confirm that manual fallback procedures are functioning.
intelligence.forecast: Without arrival metering, the yard will fill and delays will spread to vessel, rail, trucking, warehouse, and customer operations.

sources: Fictional exercise content; no live operational data.
